outcome: The overall structure of Keisler's order remains open, but a September 2025 expository paper by Malliaris (arXiv:2509.14068) discloses a new theorem, from a book manuscript in progress with Shelah, introducing a 'canonical Boolean algebra' construction and proving a chain-condition result for it (for the random graph, extended to simple theories with trivial forking); this is new machinery aimed at the structure problem, not yet published as a standalone refereed paper.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the overall structure of Keisler's order, a decades-old classification program in model theory. The triage record was correct that no result settling or substantially reshaping the overall structure appeared in the window; the two headline results it found (infinitely many classes, 2015/2018; continuum many classes / 'Keisler's order is not simple', arXiv:1906.10241, 2019) both predate 26 January 2024, as does the closely related 'Some simple theories from a Boolean algebra point of view' (Malliaris-Shelah, arXiv:2108.05314, posted August 2021, journal-published July 2023 despite carrying an 'Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 175 (2024)' volume label — I verified the PDF's own 'Available online 24 July 2023' date, so this is open_stale-adjacent and not counted as a within-window event). I searched further for anything genuinely new since the frozen date and found one item: Maryanthe Malliaris's September 2025 solo expository paper 'On ultrafilter construction' (arXiv:2509.14068, submitted 2025-09-17), which is a historical/pedagogical survey of the field but also explicitly discloses a new theorem (§14, Theorem 14.1) from a forthcoming Malliaris-Shelah book manuscript 'Ultrafilters and Theories' (cited as [Malliaris-Shelah], 'manuscript in progress'). This theorem introduces a newly defined 'canonical Boolean algebra' associated to a theory T and proves it satisfies a strong chain condition for the random graph, extending to any simple theory with trivial forking under mild parameter changes. This is squarely about the mechanisms underlying Keisler's order's structure (the algebra doesn't depend on choosing an ultrafilter jointly, unlike the 2021 construction) and is new mathematics disclosed within the window, so it counts as `progress`: a technical building-block result, not a resolution and not even a fully separate refereed paper yet. I classified it `progress` rather than `claimed` because it is not offered as a completed proof of a major open question but as an incremental theorem in an ongoing research program, presented by one of the two field-leading authors in an expository context; I did not find a subsequent standalone research paper stating and proving Theorem 14.1 in full detail, so no independent expert digestion of the full proof exists yet, but the informal nature and modest scope of the claim (a chain-condition lemma) makes 'progress' more apt than 'claimed' (which better fits a claimed resolution awaiting verification). No AI system is mentioned anywhere in any of the sources checked. I also checked and ruled out several other candidate 2024-2026 papers as out-of-scope variants (per the problem's scope rule, §3.1): Keisler measures / invariant Keisler measures (arXiv:2408.08370, arXiv:2406.00912, arXiv:2605.15870) and the Rudin-Keisler order on ultrafilters over measurable cardinals or P-points (arXiv:2601.10614, arXiv:2404.03238, arXiv:2511.19354) are distinct mathematical objects from Keisler's order (the ultrapower-saturation preorder on complete theories) despite sharing Keisler's name; none of these bear on the structure of Keisler's order itself. I also want to flag that an earlier WebSearch tool call hallucinated a '2026' date for Douglas Ulrich's 2018 paper 'Keisler's Order and Full Boolean-Valued Models' (arXiv:1810.05335) — I verified directly via WebFetch that this paper was submitted 2018-10-12 with a single version, so it is not a within-window event and I have excluded it.
competing_reading: One could argue the September 2025 survey paper's Theorem 14.1 should not count at all, on the grounds that it is announced in an expository/celebratory piece (dedicated to Shelah's birthday) rather than a dedicated research paper, and that the full proof lives only in an unpublished, unavailable book manuscript that I could not inspect — meaning this is closer to a preview or announcement than a citable, checkable result, and arguably the record should be `open` with `no_change_found: true` since no independently verifiable new theorem about the *overall* structure has actually landed. I lean toward `progress` because the theorem statement itself (with hypotheses and conclusion) is fully given in the paper, is new (not a restatement of prior work), and is clearly offered as an established fact ('Here is a first theorem from the book in progress'), not merely a promise of future work.
what_would_settle_it: Locating the full Malliaris-Shelah manuscript 'Ultrafilters and Theories' (or a subsequent standalone arXiv posting extracting Theorem 14.1 and its proof) would let me verify the proof directly and would also reveal whether later chapters of that manuscript make more substantial progress on the structure question than what is disclosed in the September 2025 survey.
